advisor.summary: Since the TCJA, §1031 deferral covers real property only — every equipment or vehicle trade-in completed after 2017 is a fully taxable disposition at the trade-in allowance, with gain up to prior depreciation recognized as ordinary recapture income. Federally the sting is usually neutralized: the replacement asset typically qualifies for 100% bonus depreciation or first-year expensing that equals or exceeds the recognized recapture. But the wash is an outcome, not a rule — it fails in states that decouple from bonus depreciation, in loss years where the offsetting deduction is trapped, and whenever the replacement costs less than the trade-in allowance. This advisory record exists to retire stale pre-2018 client expectations and to price the specific pockets where the trade is not a wash before the client signs at the dealership.
mechanics: TCJA (P.L. 115-97) amended §1031(a)(1) to reach real property only, for exchanges completed after December 31, 2017 — equipment, vehicles, machinery, and other personal property no longer qualify for deferral.

A trade-in splits into two transactions: a sale of the old asset at the trade-in allowance — a §1001 realization event, with gain up to prior depreciation taxed as §1245 ordinary recapture — and a purchase of the new asset at full invoice price with a full cost basis.

The federal offset: the replacement is generally eligible for 100% bonus depreciation under §168(k) (permanent under OBBBA for property acquired after January 19, 2025) or §179 expensing ($2,560,000 limit with a $4,090,000 phase-out for 2026), so the year-one deduction usually absorbs the recapture when the replacement costs at least as much as the allowance.
Character still matters even when the dollars wash: recapture is ordinary income reported on Form 4797, it gets no capital-gain rate, and it inflates AGI-driven phase-outs in the trade year.

Real property exchanges remain fully available — qualified intermediary, 45-day identification, 180-day closing — and Reg. §1.1031(a)-3, not the invoice description, draws the post-TCJA line on what counts as real property.

Gain on disposed equipment is ordinary recapture income up to prior depreciation, recognized in the trade year.

requirements: Every equipment trade-in reported as a disposition at the trade-in allowance on Form 4797 — never carryover-basis treatment as if pre-2018 law still applied.
Replacement eligibility for bonus or §179 confirmed — including the used-property rules — before the offset is assumed.
State conformity checked on both sides — the recapture and the replacement deduction — before calling the trade a wash.
Asset-by-asset depreciation records sufficient to compute recapture on each trade.
risks: The primary exposure is the unreported disposition: clients and legacy software habits still treat equipment trades as tax-free rollovers, and the mismatch surfaces on exam through Form 4797 and depreciation-schedule review rather than through any leading case.
State decoupling is a real current-year cost — the recapture is taxed now while the replacement deduction spreads over the state life.
Loss-year mismatch: recapture is recognized even when the offsetting bonus deduction sits trapped in a limited loss (a §461(l) interaction), turning the wash into a timing cost.
Fleet and heavy-equipment operations with continuous trade cycles now generate recapture churn that must be tracked asset by asset, every year.
Relabeling personal property as real property to force it into §1031 invites adjustment — Reg. §1.1031(a)-3 controls, not the invoice.
stateNotes: The federal wash depends entirely on the state conforming to bonus depreciation and §179 — several states decouple from or cap the deductions and tax the recapture currently, so the state answer must be priced trade by trade.

PTET interaction: recapture recognized inside a pass-through raises the entity's PTET base in the trade year while the offsetting deduction lowers it — so the net PTET effect tracks the federal wash in conforming states.

Missouri conforms to federal depreciation, including §168(k) bonus, through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121), so the wash generally holds for Missouri; note that the state's individual capital-gains subtraction does not shelter §1245 recapture, which is ordinary income, not capital gain.
reviewChecklist: Every planned trade listed with its computed §1245 recapture from the depreciation schedule.
Bonus vs. §179 election chosen with the client's state caps in mind, and the state add-back cost priced before signing.
Loss-year interactions checked — the offsetting deduction must actually be usable in the trade year.
Form 4797 reporting confirmed at filing for each trade, with the replacement's basis set at full cost.
Any real-property exchange routed through a qualified intermediary, with the 45/180-day calendar in the file.

client.teaser: Equipment trade-ins stopped being tax-free in 2018 — we keep yours from turning into a surprise.
client.headline: The new playbook for trading in equipment
plainEnglish: For decades, trading old equipment for new was tax-free. The old machine's value simply rolled into the new one. That ended in 2018. Now only real estate gets that treatment. A trade-in of trucks, machines, or gear counts as a sale.

Any value above what is left on your books is taxable income that year. The good news: you can usually deduct the full cost of the new equipment in the same year. Most of the time, the deduction cancels the tax, and the net result is close to zero.

But 'usually' is not 'always.' Some states do not allow the instant write-off. Some loss years leave the deduction stuck while the trade-in income still counts. Tell us before you trade, and we will check both sides first.
client.analogy: A store that once did even swaps now writes two receipts: one to buy your old item, one to sell you the new. Most days the receipts cancel out. We read both before you trade.
